ledger.note: 1086: Malik-Shah conquers northern Syria. 'Malik-Shah moved towards Northern Syria with his army in 1086'; Aleppo, Antioch, Edessa, Harran and Qal'at Ja'bar were captured. The page names no holders (the uqaylid-dynasty dossier records Aleppo's loss in 1086).

1086: Malik-Shah retakes Ganja. 'Malik-Shah launched a campaign in 1086 and removed Fadl from power again' (Shaddadids page); the Malik-Shah page: 'Ganja, where Fadl III was based, was besieged and captured. Fadl III was taken prisoner.'

1087: Bukhara and Samarkand come under Seljuk rule. In 1087 he took Kara-Khanid castles, 'especially Bukhara, Samarkand, Balasagun, Isfijab and Kashgar'; the Turkistan Region 'was brought under Seljuk rule in 1089'. The Kara-Khanid khans stay in place (the Qatwan page calls the Kara-Khanid Khanate the Seljuks' vassal in 1141), so vassalage is my reading. Balasagun, Isfijab and Kashgar lie beyond Cliopatria's eastern edge (73.95 E).

region.text: Balasagun, Isfijab and Kashgar, the Eastern lands to which the Seljuk campaign reached

ledger.note: 1087: Malik-Shah's Transoxiana expedition reaches the Eastern Kara-Khanids. 'In 1087, due to internal unrest in Turkestan, Malik-Shah decided to organize another expedition to Transoxiana' and 'captured many castles belonging to the Kara-Khanids, especially Bukhara, Samarkand, Balasagun, Isfijab and Kashgar' (Malik-Shah page). Bukhara and Samarkand are the vassal event above; Balasagun, Isfijab and Kashgar are the Eastern Khanate's. Mirrors eastern-kara-khanids /ledger/2.

region.text: Balasagun, Isfijab and Kashgar, the Eastern lands to which the Seljuk campaign reached

ledger.note: 1089: the expedition ends with the Eastern khan a vassal. 'the entire Turkistan Region, up to the borders of China, was brought under Seljuk rule in 1089' (Malik-Shah page). Mirrors eastern-kara-khanids /ledger/3.

region.text: Balasagun, Isfijab and Kashgar, the Eastern lands to which the Seljuk campaign reached

ledger.note: 1089: the Eastern Kara-Khanid khan becomes a Seljuk vassal. 'the Eastern Kara-Khanid ruler Hasan ibn Suleiman came to Malik-Shah and agreed to be his vassal' (Malik-Shah page, in the 1087 paragraph with no year of its own; 1089 is the page's year for Turkistan). The eastern-kara-khanids dossier, quoting the Kara-Khanid page, has the Eastern Khanate a Seljuk vassal 'for only a short time'. Mirrors eastern-kara-khanids /ledger/4.

1090: the Nizari Ismailis end Ziyarid rule in Tabaristan. 'the Nizari Ismaili state under Hassan-i Sabbah invaded and conquered his domains', 'which ended Ziyarid rule in Tabaristan' (Ziyarid page). The page does not say whether the tribute of 1041 was still paid; the year is the end of the tributary state.

region.text: Balasagun, Isfijab and Kashgar, the Eastern lands to which the Seljuk campaign reached

ledger.note: 1092: a bridging year. The pages give no end for the short Seljuk vassalage of the Eastern Khanate; Malik-Shah died on 19 November 1092 (reign dates, Malik-Shah I page) and the empire split (Seljuk Empire page). Mirrors eastern-kara-khanids /ledger/5.

region.text: the Levant: the Damascus and Aleppo Seljuk lines

ledger.counterpart: Seljuk Syria (Tutush I; Damascus and Aleppo lines)
ledger.note: 1092: Malik-Shah dies and the empire splits. 'When Malik-Shah I died in 1092, the empire split' as his brother and four sons quarrelled; Tutush I was killed fighting Berkyaruq in February 1096. The Seljuk dynasty page's infobox lists separate seats at Damascus (1076-1104) and Aleppo (1086-1117) and, for Rum, Nicaea (1077-1097); the Levant is my reading of 'the split'. Jerusalem and Damascus were gained in 1073 and 1076 and northern Syria in 1086 (ledger); what the split hands over is the Levant of Cliopatria's shape.

1118: Sanjar becomes sultan and the empire has two seats. Muhammad I Tapar died on 4 April 1118; Sanjar's reign began 18 April 1118 (Sanjar page); infobox: Merv (1118-1153, eastern) and Hamadan (1118-1194, western); 'Isfahan ceased to be an imperial residence' (Seljuk Empire page).

1121: the Seljuks are routed at Didgori on 12 August. The Seljuk Empire page gives the battle only; that Georgia ceased to be a vassal is my inference from it. The Battle of Didgori page (opened 2026-10-25) says nothing of a vassalage or tribute: Mahmud II sent an expedition after complaints from Muslim merchants in Tbilisi, Ganja and Dmanisi, and 'In the first half of 1121, the Georgians twice attacked the Seljuks' in the Emirate of Ganja; the battle was fought 'on August 12, 1121'.
1127: Zengi is made governor of Mosul. The Seljuk Empire page: Imad al-Din Zengi was named Governor of Mosul (the zengid-dynasty dossier: atabeg of Mosul in charge of al-Jazira and northern Syria).

1135: Sanjar's army enters Ghaznavid land and reinstates Bahram Shah. 'In August or September 1135, the Seljuk army mobilized and entered the Ghaznavid Empire's territory'; Bahram, 'a vassal of the Great Seljuk Empire, failed to pay taxes'; Sanjar 'pardoned him and reinstated him'; Bahram had 'succeeded to the throne as the Seljuk's vassal' (the page dates neither his accession nor 1117).

region.text: Iraq from Basra in the south to the edges of Mosul in the north, the part inside the Seljuk shape

ledger.note: 1136: Iraq passes from the Seljuk sultans to the caliph's state. Seljuk Empire page: 'Iraq remained under Seljuk control until 1135', 'The Seljuk control of the Abbasids ended in 1135', 'Mas'ud briefly recaptured Baghdad in the Siege of Baghdad (1136)' and the next caliph, al-Muqtafi (1136-1160), 'managed to restore a high degree of independence'. Al-Muqtafi page (fx-06): proclaimed caliph on 17 September 1136 after Mas'ud's forces besieged the city; in 1148 he 'successfully fought off a group of Seljuk generals' who had rebelled against Mas'ud; after Mas'ud's death (the page dates the next steps after October 1152) he 'seized Wasit and al-Hilla' and won Suleiman-Shah's 'pledge not to interfere in Iraq'; in 1157 the Seljuks under Muhammad besieged Baghdad and gave up. Abbasid Caliphate page: by the end of al-Muqtafi's reign (1160) the caliph 'controlled a state stretching from Basra in the south to the edges of Mosul in the north'. Moved by fx-06 from 1160 to 1136, the year the Seljuk Empire page ends the Seljuk control of Iraq; the Al-Muqtafi page shows Mas'ud still pressing the caliph until 1152, so 1153 is the later reading, and the Abbasid page's formal independence is 1165 (confidence 2). The abbasid-caliphate dossier (not edited here) still draws Baghdad only to 1159 and has its mirror gain at 1160: handoff.

1138: Sanjar marches on Khwarezm. 'In 1138, Sanjar marched with his army to Khwarezm and defeated Atsiz and his army in the Battle of Hazorasp' (Atsiz 'rebelled openly against his suzerain' that year, Atsiz page).

1139: Mosul and the Jazira leave the Seljuk shape. Cliopatria's Great Seljuk row drops the Jazira (93% to 8%) and Syria in 1139; the Seljuk Empire page records only Zengi's appointment in 1127 and, for 1157, that 'the Atabegs became effectively independent'. The year is the shape's; the page is silent.

1141: Atsiz occupies Merv, Nishapur and Sarakhs. 'Atsiz took advantage of the defeat to invade Khorasan, occupying Merv, Nishapur, and Sarakhs' (Atsiz page; the defeat is Qatwan, 9 September 1141, and the page gives no year or month for the invasion itself). Mirrors khwarezmid-dynasty /ledger/3.

region.text: Transoxiana east of the Syr Darya, with Samarkand

ledger.note: 1141: Sanjar loses Transoxiana at Qatwan. Qara Khitai won on 9 September 1141, 'a decisive defeat for the Seljuks'; Yelu Dashi made Mahmud's brother Ibrahim ruler of Samarkand; Sanjar lost 'all Seljuk territory east of the Syr Darya' (Sanjar page).

1141: the Kara-Khanids pass from the Seljuks to the Qara Khitai. The Battle of Qatwan page lists them as the Seljuks' vassal; after the battle Yelu Dashi appoints Ibrahim at Samarkand and lets the Burhans keep Bukhara.
1142: Sanjar expels Atsiz from Khorasan. 'In 1142, Atsiz was expelled from Khorasan by Sanjar' (Atsiz page). Mirrors khwarezmid-dynasty /ledger/4.

1143: Sanjar subdues Khwarezm again. 'Sanjar then marched to Khwarezm with his army in 1143' after Atsiz had taken Khwarezm in 1141 and been 'expelled from Khorasan by Sanjar' in 1142 (Atsiz page: Sanjar forced Atsiz back into vassalage).

1143: Atsiz is made a vassal again. Sanjar's 1143 march (Sanjar page) forced Atsiz back into vassalage (Atsiz page); Sanjar 'marched on Khwarezm with his army in 1147' when Atsiz 'became rebellious again', with no result on either page.
1152: the Ghurids take Herat. 'the Ghurids led by Ala al-Din Husayn, a vassal of the Ghaznavids, captured Herat and advanced towards Balkh'.

1152: Khwarezm leaves the Seljuk shape. Cliopatria's Khwarezmid row returns in 1152 after a gap in 1147-1151; the Atsiz page has him recapture Jand from a Qara Khitai band in April 1152 and pay tribute to the Qara Khitai 'until his death' (1156), and gives no end of the vassalage to Sanjar. The year is the shape's.

1152: Sanjar defeats the Ghurids at Nab, 24 June. 'The two armies met at a place called Nab near Herat on June 24, 1152'; 'Ala al-Din Husayn was decisively defeated and taken prisoner by Sanjar'. (The ghurid-dynasty dossier has the Ghurids take Herat for good in 1175.)

1153: Balkh falls to the Oghuz. 'In 1153, Amir Qumach was delegated command as governor of Balkh' and attacked the Oghuz with 12,000 cavalry but 'was defeated and forced to flee to Merv'; the page does not describe Balkh or Tokharistan afterwards, so the loss of the region is my reading. The event was dated 1152 (confidence 1, the Cliopatria shape's year); the page has Balkh still Seljuk in 1153, so it moves to 1153 and keyframe 1152b holds Bactria for 1152. [Repair, me-09-a author, 2026-10-25: re-dated 1152 -> 1153 and tied to the Oghuz revolt; the counterpart was 'Balkh and Tokharistan (holder not named on the page)']

1153: the Oghuz defeat Sanjar and take him prisoner. 'in April 1153 at the Battle of Muharram, which ended in a defeat for the Seljuks'; 'Sanjar was captured during the battle and held in captivity until 1156'; he escaped in the fall of 1156. [Reviewer me-09-a, 2026-10-25: counterpart 'oghuz-turks' -> a name: that dossier is the Oghuz Yabghu state, which ends in 1055; the Ahmad Sanjar page calls the 1153 rebels 'the Seljuks' own tribe, the Oghuz Turks'.]

1157: Sanjar dies at Merv, 8 May. 'Sanjar died in 1157 and was buried in Merv'; 'The death of Sanjar meant the end of the Seljuq dynasty as an empire' and the Atabegs 'became effectively independent' (Seljuk Empire page). [Reviewer me-09-a, 2026-10-25: counterpart 'oghuz-turks' -> a name: that dossier is the Oghuz Yabghu state, which ends in 1055; the Ahmad Sanjar page calls the 1153 rebels 'the Seljuks' own tribe, the Oghuz Turks'.]

ledger.counterpart: Turkic and Turkmen rulers of Khorasan (Oghuz, Ay-Aba at Nishapur)
ledger.note: 1157: Khorasan passes out of Seljuk hands. 'After his death, Turkic rulers, Turkmen tribal forces, and other secondary powers competed for Khorasan'; Tekish wins it piece by piece in 1174-1193 (khwarezmid-dynasty ledger), the Ghurids at Herat in 1175.

1157: the Ghaznavid vassalage ends with Sanjar. The Sanjar page gives no end to the Ghaznavid tie; 'When Sanjar died in 1157, the empire fractured even further' (Seljuk Empire page). The year is Sanjar's death.
1187: the Kerman Seljuk line ends. Infobox: 'Kerman/Bardasir (1041-1186); Bam (1186-1187)'; the dependency on the sultans is not dated on any opened page after 1074.
1193: Tekish takes Ray. 'Tekish captured Ray in January 1193, followed by the Tabrak citadel after 2 day siege'; Toghrul III then offered to become a vassal and hand over Ray.

region.text: Rayy, Hamadan and Isfahan: Persian Iraq

ledger.note: 1194: Tughril III is killed at the Battle of Rayy, 4 March. Tughril III attacked on 4 March 1194 and was defeated and killed; the Khwarazmians conquered Persian Iraq, including Isfahan, by 25 June 1194 (Tekish page). Infobox: 'Battle of Ray and the supplantation by the Khwarazmian Empire: 1194'.
1194: the struggle for Rayy ends with the Seljuk defeat of 4 March.

region.text: Persian Iraq, the last Great Seljuk land

ledger.note: 1194: the Great Seljuk state ends at the Battle of Rayy. 'the Seljuk Empire finally collapsed in 1194' (Seljuk Empire page); Seljuk rule continued only in Anatolia (Rum). Cliopatria draws the row to 1201.

wars.name: Battle of Dandanaqan
wars.outcome: Decisive Seljuk victory on 23 May 1040 near Merv; Khorasan, Herat, Sistan and Ghur pass to the Seljuks.
wars.note: Fighting begins at Nasa in 1035 (seljuk-dynasty ledger).

wars.name: Tughril's conquests in Iraq and Persia
wars.outcome: Gorgan and Tabaristan (1041-1042), Rayy (1042-1043), Isfahan (1052), Azerbaijan (1054), Baghdad (1055) and Mosul (1057) fall; Tughril receives the title 'King of the East and the West' in 1058.
wars.note: Not a Wikipedia title; a grouping of the Tughril page's dated steps.

wars.name: Battle of Manzikert
wars.outcome: Seljuk victory on 26 August 1071; Romanos IV taken prisoner for a week; Turkish settlement of Anatolia follows, outside the sultan's own border.

wars.name: Seljuk-Georgian wars
wars.outcome: Alp Arslan subjugates Tbilisi (1065); Seljuk amirs are beaten by George II (1073); Malik-Shah's second campaign (1078-1079) and George II's 1088 submission at Isfahan; the Seljuks are routed at Didgori on 12 August 1121.
wars.note: No border line is drawn; Georgia is a vassal 1079-1121 in the ledger (the dates of the end are inferred).

wars.name: Qavurd's revolt and the Battle of Kerj Abu Dulaf
wars.outcome: Malik-Shah wins the three-day battle near Hamadan in 1073 and has Qavurd strangled; in 1074 he besieges Bardsir and stops when Sultan-Shah 'begged for forgiveness'.

wars.name: Malik-Shah's Syrian campaign
wars.outcome: Aleppo, Antioch, Edessa, Harran and Qal'at Ja'bar captured; the emirs of Anatolia fail at Nicaea c. 1088-1091.

wars.name: Malik-Shah's Transoxiana expedition

zones.text: Balasagun, Isfijab and Kashgar, the Eastern lands to which the Seljuk campaign reached

wars.outcome: Malik-Shah takes Kara-Khanid castles (Bukhara, Samarkand, Balasagun, Isfijab, Kashgar); the Eastern khan Hasan ibn Suleiman becomes his vassal and the Turkistan Region 'up to the borders of China' is under Seljuk rule in 1089.
wars.note: Bukhara and Samarkand (western Kara-Khanids) are the vassal event of 1087; the Eastern lands are the contest of 1087-1089.

wars.name: Seljuk war of succession (Berkyaruq against Tutush)
wars.outcome: Tutush I was killed in battle against Berkyaruq in February 1096; Sanjar was made governor of Khorasan in 1097.
wars.note: Where the fighting lay is not on the page.

wars.name: First Crusade
wars.outcome: The Seljuk Empire infobox dates the First Crusade 1095-1099; no page opened gives a Great Seljuk action in it (the Levant is the Syrian Seljuk lines' ground in the correction).

wars.name: Sanjar's Khwarezm campaigns
wars.outcome: Hazarasp (1138), Atsiz's raid on Khorasan (1141-1142), Sanjar's march of 1143 and again of 1147 keep Khwarezm a vassal.

wars.name: Battle of Qatwan
wars.outcome: Decisive Qara Khitai victory on 9 September 1141; the Seljuks lose Transoxiana and Khwarezm turns to the Qara Khitai.

wars.name: Ghurid-Seljuk clash at Nab
wars.outcome: Sanjar defeats and captures Ala al-Din Husayn at Nab on 24 June 1152.

wars.name: Oghuz revolt and the capture of Sanjar
wars.outcome: Sanjar is defeated in April 1153, held until 1156, escapes and dies at Merv in 1157; Khorasan is left to Turkic and Turkmen rulers.

wars.name: Khwarezmid conquest of Persian Iraq (Battle of Rayy)
wars.outcome: Tekish takes Ray in January 1193, defeats and kills Tughril III on 4 March 1194 and holds Persian Iraq by 25 June 1194.

certainty.note: No frontier of the Great Seljuk state is fixed by treaty on any page opened: the steppe and desert edges, the Byzantine, Georgian and Crusader frontiers and the vassal tints are all approximate. The Abbasid caliph's recognition of Seljuk rule over Khorasan (by 1046) and the Didgori and Qatwan battle lines are the only dated anchors.

notes: Pages: nine for 16 ledger arcs (budget 9): Seljuk Empire, Seljuk dynasty, Battle of Dandanaqan, Tughril, Alp Arslan, Malik-Shah I, Ahmad Sanjar, Battle of Qatwan and Ala ad-Din Tekish; the Atsiz page (opened for the Khwarezmid dossier) is cited once, for the 1152 vassal_end. Failed titles: none for this state. One state or two: the Seljuk Dynasty row (990-1039) and this row are the same Seljuk state (see seljuk-dynasty notes); a reviewer may merge. Cliopatria rows to correct: the row ends 1201 but the state ends 4 March 1194; 1040-1045 and 1046-1055 hold Fars, Kerman, Isfahan, Azerbaijan years early; 1056 and 1066 miss Armenia (1064); 1085 holds Anatolia (the Rum seat is Nicaea from 1077); 1094-1138 hold the Levant that the Damascus and Aleppo Seljuk lines held; 1157-1187 hold Khorasan that the sultans lost at Sanjar's death. NOT corrected though doubtful: Iraq in the 1139-1201 shapes (the Seljuk Empire page says Iraq stayed Seljuk until 1135 and that Seljuk control over the Abbasids ended then), Fars in 1046-1062, the eastern edge at 70.6-73.95 E in 1066-1146, the Gulf coast (Malik-Shah's 1075 army against the Qarmatians in Bahrain is on the Malik-Shah page and is not coded). Page disagreements: Khorasan to the Ghurids in 1192 (Sanjar page, 'finally conquered by the Ghurids in 1192') against 1200 (Seljuk Empire page: the Ghurids took control of all Khorasan after Tekish died) and Tekish's capture of Merv in December 1193 (Tekish page); Isfahan as capital 1051 (infobox) against Tughril's entry in Muharram 1052 (Tughril page); Alp Arslan's death 24 November (text) against 15 December 1072 (infobox); the Seljuk dynasty page says the Great Seljuk Empire was 'established' after the 1050/51 siege of Isfahan, the Seljuk Empire page 1037. Months converted from a Hijri date by me: December 1055 (Baghdad). Native names are from general knowledge, not from a page. Counterparts needing dossiers: the Kerman Seljuk sultanate (1041-1187), the Seljuks of Syria (Tutush's Damascus line 1076-1104 and the Aleppo line 1086-1117), the Eldiguzids (Atabegs of Azerbaijan), the Artuqids, Mu'ayyid Ay-Aba's emirate of Nishapur (to 1174), Sultan-Shah's Khorasan (1181-1193, see khwarezmid-dynasty) and the Emirate of Tbilisi. Gazetteer names: 'Persian Iraq' (Iraq-i Ajam; used as a union of Iranian provinces: Hamadan, Esfahan, Markazi, Qom, Tehran, Alborz, Qazvin, Zanjan).
